title: Telstra Health: Expanding Product into New Market
lead: Telstra Health aimed to expand its Virtual Health Platform into the aged-care market, but needed a clearer understanding of frontline professionals’ needs to ensure the product addressed real challenges. As the Product Designer, I led customer discovery, validated proposed ideas with aged-care professionals, and worked with product, clinical and engineering teams to prioritise and design three key capabilities: multi-party video consultations, clinical notes and task management. The resulting designs helped shape the platform for aged-care workflows and supported Telstra Health in securing customer deals.

blocks.text: Due to company confidentiality policies, some project details and product screens cannot be shared publicly. If you'd like to learn more about my work and design process, feel free to get in touch.

Telstra Health's leadership recognised growing demand in the aged-care market, where providers were facing increasing pressure to coordinate care across residential and community settings. This presented an opportunity to position Virtual Health Platform (VHP) more strongly in the market and expand its adoption among aged-care providers.

When I joined the project, the Product Manager and team had already developed an initial product vision informed by market research and competitor analysis. More than 20 potential capabilities had been identified as opportunities for the platform.

However, they hadn't yet spoken directly with frontline professionals. They didn't know how they managed their day-to-day responsibilities, where their biggest challenges were or which proposed capabilities would deliver the most value.
The team had a clear market opportunity and plenty of ideas, but needed a better understanding of customer needs to determine the right product direction.

I was brought in to help shape the design strategy for VHP's expansion into aged care. With an initial product vision already in place, my role was to bring customer perspectives into the process, validate the proposed ideas against real-world workflows and identify the capabilities that would deliver the most value.

I worked across customer discovery, product prioritisation and experience design, bridging customer needs, business priorities and technical considerations to turn the opportunity into practical product solutions.
Uncovering the real problems
I designed two customer workshops to understand how aged-care professionals managed their day-to-day work, where they experienced friction and what support they needed.

I explored their existing workflows before introducing the team's proposed capabilities, so their feedback wasn't influenced by our assumptions. I then used prioritisation exercises and storyboards to identify the most valuable opportunities and understand how potential solutions would fit into their work.
Turning insights into product priorities
I synthesised the workshop findings and played them back to the team to establish a shared understanding of customer needs.

Working with product, clinical and engineering stakeholders, I evaluated the opportunities against customer value, technical feasibility and implementation complexity. This helped us move beyond a long list of ideas and agree on three priorities for the initial product scope: multi-party video consultations, clinical notes and task management.
Design and deliver implementation-ready solutions
I translated the agreed capabilities into user flows and interface designs, working through interaction logic and different design options with stakeholders.

I considered edge cases and clinical safety throughout the process, using AI-assisted exploration to challenge assumptions and coded prototypes to communicate complex interactions. I also validated the end-to-end designs with customers before preparing annotated Figma specifications for engineering handover.

sections.label: Key Decisions and Trade-offs I Made

blocks.text: The solutions didn't come together instantly. Throughout the process, I explored different options, challenged assumptions and weighed trade-offs to work towards the right direction for both customers and the business.

items.label: Putting customer needs before product assumptions
items.text: I separated workflow discovery from capability validation during the workshops. This gave participants space to describe their actual challenges before seeing our proposed solutions, helping us avoid leading their feedback and uncover needs we might otherwise have missed.

items.label: Balancing customer value with technical feasibility
items.text: Not every customer need could fit into the initial scope. I worked with product, clinical and engineering stakeholders to weigh customer value against technical complexity and implementation effort. This helped us prioritise the capabilities that delivered the greatest value while keeping the MVP focused and achievable within a shorter delivery timeframe.

items.label: Using AI to challenge my thinking
items.text: I used AI as a thinking partner to challenge initial requirements, explore alternative approaches and identify potential gaps, user scenarios and edge cases. Rather than accepting its suggestions at face value, I applied my own design judgement to evaluate the options and decide on the final direction.

items.label: Prioritising clarity in clinical workflows
items.text: In clinical environments, ambiguity can lead to confusion and mistakes. I worked with the Clinical Safety Officer to consider how information was presented and how users interacted with critical workflows. For example, I explored different ways to display patient identity and consultation participants during scheduling to make their roles clearer.

blocks.text: In this client engagement, I brought clarity to the problem space, helping the team make informed product decisions that aligned with real market needs. I then delivered designs for 3 key capabilities to support VHP's expansion into the aged-care market.

items.label: Multi-party video consultations
items.text: Supporting virtual consultations involving multiple participants.

items.label: Clinical notes
items.text: Improving access to patient information and clinical documentation.

items.label: Task management
items.text: Supporting clearer task coordination and ownership.

blocks.text: My design deliverables were presented to and validated by customers, helping Telstra Health secure deals to expand its services across aged-care facilities.
The capabilities were released in stages, with implementation considerations shaping the rollout. The work helped establish how VHP could evolve to better support the needs of aged-care providers.

title: Telstra Health: Designing with AI
lead: As a Product Designer at Cognizant, I drove design across Telstra Health's portfolio of 30+ established products, working with cross-functional teams to understand user and market needs, shape requirements and deliver solutions. One of my key contributions was leading discovery and end-to-end design for a new capability on a virtual health platform, helping extend the product into new markets and attract more customers. Beyond traditional design workflows, I've integrated AI into my process through product-specific DESIGN.md files, AI agents in Figma and code-based prototyping. Adding multi-factor authentication (MFA) to a decade-old legacy product demonstrates how this approach helps navigate technical complexity and accelerate design exploration.

sections.label: Why design needs a bridge here

blocks.text: As a Product Designer in TH, I worked across more than 30 of their classic products. The biggest challenges I faced was designing products with significant accumulated technical debt, where technical constraints weren't always discussed upfront.

Many of these products had years of accumulated architecture, technical decisions and constraints. However, much of this knowledge wasn't formally documented, making it difficult for product managers, business analysts and stakeholders to understand how the systems worked and make informed decisions.
From a design perspective, this created 3 key challenges that hindered delivery:

items.label: Requirement Definition
items.text: The beginning of every design initiative usually starts with draft requirements, but the technical constraints and implementation complexity aren't always considered upfront. Without tangible artefacts to visualise the proposed solution, stakeholders struggle to align on requirements, leading to frequent changes and design rework.

items.label: Knowledge Gaps
items.text:
Product managers, POs and BAs change frequently, and there isn't always one point of contact who understands the entire product.

With limited documentation and restricted access to the environment, teams often lack a shared understanding of the existing architecture and interaction patterns. This makes decision-making difficult, as even a small change can require significant technical effort. Teams also need to carefully consider the time and resources available within each sprint to meet delivery deadlines.

items.label: Delayed Decisions
items.text: Design directions often depend on engineering teams validating feasibility. However, due to time constraints, these reviews often happen after the designs are completed. This can lead to further clarification of requirements, revisiting design decisions and additional rework, eventually delaying delivery.

blocks.text: Looking across these challenges, I realised they were connected by one recurring issue.
Theme: Too much uncertainty was being carried into the design process.

sections.label: Rethinking the Design Process with AI

blocks.text: We often made decisions based on incomplete context or a clear understanding of how things would work in practice.

I started questioning how I, as a designer, could connect all the dots by bringing more context and technical understanding into the design process earlier. So to get everyone on the same page, simplify complex problems and help teams make better decisions.

That's where I began experimenting with AI, not simply to generate designs faster, but to give teams a clearer picture of the product and proposed solutions. This helped improve alignment and make delivery more efficient.
I wanted to use it to make different design possibilities tangible, strengthen the thinking behind each decision and communicate design intent more clearly to stakeholders and leadership.
This led me to rethink the design process and identify 3 key opportunities for AI to reduce uncertainty and improve team alignment.

items.label: Broaden Design Exploration
items.text: I used AI to explore different design directions and generate alternative solutions. This gives stakeholders tangible options to compare, discuss trade-offs and align on what should be included before committing to a solution.

items.label: Make Product Behaviour Visible
items.text: I explored using AI to turn complex user journeys into interactive prototypes. By presenting prototypes instead of static screens in Figma, I helped the team better understand how the product works, how users navigate between screens and how different interactions behave.

items.label: Improve Design Handoff
items.text: I went beyond static design files by using AI to create more functional and detailed handoff artefacts. This helped engineers understand the intended interactions, screen transitions and underlying logic, reducing guesswork during implementation.

blocks.text: From Explore, Understand to Implement
The goal was to bring clarity into the design process earlier, helping teams make better informed decisions and move into development with greater alignment.
Explore: What are the possible solutions, and what are the trade-offs?
Understand: How should the product and user journeys actually work?
Communicate: How can engineering implement the intended experience accurately?
To demonstrate how I applied these ideas in practice, I'd like to share a project involving the introduction of Multi-Factor Authentication to an established healthcare product.
The product had been built over many years, with limited design documentation or existing Figma resources to work from.
As a result, the team faced challenges understanding the existing product behaviour, clarifying requirements and aligning on how the new experience should work.

I saw an opportunity to use AI to make these discussions more tangible, explore different solutions and help the team reach alignment earlier. To bring this approach into practice, I structured the workflow into 3 stages, using AI to support each stage of the design process.
Stage 01: Establish the Design Foundation

Through preliminary research, I found that the product was a legacy application built entirely with Microsoft WinForms, with no existing Figma library or design documentation. Before exploring new design solutions with AI, I needed to establish a shared design foundation that reflected the product's existing UI patterns. I used AI to document Microsoft's WinForms conventions and translate them into reusable Figma components through MCP. I then created `DESIGN.md` to define explicit design rules and constraints, providing AI with the context needed to generate more consistent and product-aligned designs.
Stage 02: Broaden Design Exploration

With the design foundation in place, the next challenge was exploring how the new feature could work across different user stories. As I started, I found gaps between the requirements and what was needed to create a user friendly experience. Some edge cases and conditions were still undefined. I first identified those gaps and made assumptions where requirements were missing. Then I used Claude and Figma MCP to quickly generate design variations directly in Figma. This helped me visualise the flows, validate my thinking and compare different approaches before finalising a solution. 

Throughout the process, I didn't simply rely on AI generated designs. I refined them myself and balanced usability with technical constraints. By the time I brought the designs to stakeholders for validation, I had already worked through much of the thinking. This helped reduce uncertainty and minimise potential rework during development.
Stage 03:Validate Through Prototyping

With the design direction agreed upon, I moved on to turning the Figma designs into a working MFA prototype using Claude Code.

I shared the key screens and interaction requirements with Claude, asking it to build an HTML prototype covering the journey from initial MFA setup through to verification, including different edge cases.

Instead of relying on static screens to explain the experience, I could now walk stakeholders and leadership through the actual interactions. This helped them better understand my design intent and the reasoning behind my design decisions.

By combining AI-assisted design exploration, Figma integration and code-based prototyping, I completed the design reasoning and supporting artefacts within a week. More importantly, the team could evaluate realistic options, resolve open questions and align on the intended experience much earlier. This helped the project move into development sooner and ultimately meet its conformance deadline two weeks ahead of schedule.

items.label: DELIVERY IMPACT
items.text: Delivered designs 2 weeks ahead of the conformance deadline.

items.label: STAKEHOLDER ALIGNMENT
items.text: Clearer decisions through tangible prototypes.

items.label: DEVELOPMENT READINESS
items.text: Reduced ambiguity in requirements and interactions.

items.label: Reduced Design Rework
items.text: Reduced rework through earlier decisions and clearer requirements.

blocks.text: Building is no longer the bottleneck

The gap between an imagined interaction and a working artefact is now small enough to build it, show it and change it within the same meeting. The question shift from "can we have more options?" to "which option do we pick?"
Artefacts close the gap between teams

A product manager, clinician or engineer who can't picture an edge case can walk through it in a prototype. Alignment happens earlier and with less rework, and I can tell a clearer story: here is the problem, here are the options, here is the one we chose and why.

I believe a Human-in-the-Loop approach is essential when designing with AI. Rather than allowing AI to operate independently, I keep human judgement involved throughout the process to establish guardrails, guide, review and validate its outputs, ensuring the work remains grounded in real user needs and context.

In this project, all AI-generated outputs have been validated against the platform's actual behaviour and technical constraints. A design guide is only as reliable as the sources and evidence behind it, while recommendations affecting authentication, security and patient data still require appropriate stakeholder and clinical safety review.

Similarly, AI-assisted prototypes are valuable for exploring ideas and accelerating discussions, but they cannot replace formal requirements, specifications or engineering decisions. Their purpose is to help teams evaluate options and trade-offs before committing to a solution.
AI can generate possibilities. Human judgement turns them into solutions that matter to people.

title: AI-Powered Live Market Experimentation Platform
lead: Heatseeker is an AI-powered SaaS platform that enables rapid market experimentation through live tests on social media. It helps businesses uncover what truly resonates with their audience, optimise messaging, and confidently invest in high-potential ideas. By leveraging real-time customer insights, Heatseeker turns gut instincts into data-validated strategies, accelerating growth and reducing time-to-market.

blocks.text: Brought on as a contractor, I was responsible for kickstarting the design of the AI Persona feature—leading the full UX process from research and ideation to prototyping and developer hand-off. I collaborated closely with the product team to define user goals and pain points, mapped key user flows, and designed wireframes and high-fidelity prototypes.

I delivered an MVP that laid a solid foundation for the design team, enabling them to further evolve the feature based on user needs. This helped the team move forward with clarity and direction, ensuring the product delivers actionable, data-driven insights to its users.
Due to company policy, much of my work on this project remains confidential. Feel free to reach out if you’d like to learn more.

Throughout my career as a product designer, I’ve collaborated closely with marketers and business owners, and I’ve seen firsthand the constraints they face, limited time, budget, and access to real data, when making strategic decisions. Personas are commonly used to align marketing efforts with customer needs and help teams across product lines better understand their audience. In early discovery interviews, users expressed frustration with the manual persona creation process, describing it as time-consuming, subjective, and often disconnected from real customer behaviour. Without data-backed personas, teams risk misaligned strategies and missed opportunities, underscoring the need for a faster, more reliable, and actionable solution.

No matter how many times I start a design process, I always begin with research. It helps me understand the problem space, uncover opportunities, and gain the context needed to inform effective design decisions. For this project, I studied established persona frameworks to learn how marketers traditionally build personas. I also conducted competitor analysis to identify what existing tools do well and where they fall short, helping me define clear opportunities and position our product more strategically.

blocks.caption: Competitor Analysis – insights from analysing existing persona-generating tools

items.label: PersonaGenerator
items.text: This tool requires users to manually define each persona, which can be time-consuming. However, its export feature is well-designed, making it easy to share the persona documents with team members for collaboration.

items.label: UserPersona.Dev
items.text: It uses AI to generate personas based on provided context; however, the resulting profiles often feel artificial, raising concerns about their accuracy. This makes it difficult for users to confidently rely on the personas for decision-making.

items.label: FounderPal
items.text: Another AI-powered persona generator, but the key question remains: how accurate is it? Without supporting data, users may doubt whether the generated personas truly represent their target audience, risking misguided decisions.

blocks.text: I collaborated with the CPO and consulted clients to gather requirements for the persona feature. This informed which data and AI modules to use and what information would be most valuable. Throughout the process, I began developing a mindset that I believe every designer should embrace: asking questions and seeking clarity whenever possible. Doing so ensures we truly consider users' needs at every stage of the design process.
“Good design starts with good questions. Curiosity is how we uncover real user needs and design with intention.”

Together, we developed a solution and created a standardised prompt for the LLM to generate persona outputs, providing marketers with an intuitive, data-backed way to build accurate personas that enhance audience targeting and drive conversions.
Before diving into visual design, I always start with sketching and wireframing. This step is crucial for organising my thoughts and exploring different ways to present information effectively.

For the AI persona feature, the key design challenge was maintaining simplicity. Since all information is data-driven, it was important to avoid overwhelming users with complex visuals. Each time I created wireframes, I focused on clearly structuring the LLM-generated outputs in the UI. I then gathered feedback from the team iteratively to ensure the design was informed by real input, not assumptions.

I prototyped 8 iterations to validate assumptions around persona navigation, data display, and how users read and interpret the content. I learned that prototyping is not just about gathering feedback or testing the product; it’s about clearly defining what information you want from users, how you plan to collect it, and which aspects of the design you aim to evaluate. Without a clear strategy, prototyping can become aimless and inefficient. Working in a startup environment allowed me to continuously apply this strategic mindset, iterating designs multiple times based on solid user feedback to refine and improve the product.

sections.label: From Vision to MVP in Three Weeks

blocks.text: This feature is still actively evolving. The MVP I designed has successfully attracted interest from clients like Medibank, HCF, and ADMA, who see strong potential in the tool. During client pitches, the AI-generated language in the personas resonated strongly, prompting several “aha” moments. Following these sessions, we gathered valuable feedback, which I analysed to identify future design directions and uncover new opportunities. These insights will guide the next iteration phase, with a focus on improving usability, refining data presentation, and expanding functionality to better support marketing teams.

items.label: User pain point
items.text: Client feedback revealed that different product lines often created separate, unaligned personas due to siloed marketing experiments. Without real audience data, these personas were largely assumption-based, making them unreliable and inconsistent. This prevented teams from identifying behavioural patterns or communication tone, ultimately hindering their ability to craft targeted, effective messaging.

items.label: Goal
items.text: To create a unified, data-driven persona system that helps teams generate consistent, accurate, and actionable customer profiles across product lines, enabling more aligned marketing strategies, clearer audience understanding, and more effective, targeted messaging.

items.label: Design solution
items.text:
- Generate actionable insights into customers’ backgrounds, needs, and behaviours to support strategic decision-making.
- Link live data points to persona attributes, increasing credibility and confidence in the output.
- Enable cross-team collaboration by providing a unified persona format accessible to multiple product lines.
- Support deeper exploration of customer motivations and pain points to uncover opportunities for alignment and growth.

blocks.text: Based on additional feedback collected from users, I’ve analysed the data to identify future design directions and uncover new opportunities for improvement. These insights will inform the next phase of iteration, focusing on enhancing usability, refining data presentation, and expanding functionality to better support marketing teams.

Working on this project helped me uncover a deeper challenge in designing AI-powered experiences: while AI can automate and accelerate tasks like persona generation, it often lacks the nuance, emotion, and context that create a genuine human connection. I realised that bridging the gap between AI output and real user experience isn't just about functionality — it's about trust, relatability, and relevance. Many users shared that the personas felt too generic, making it hard to see their real customers reflected in the results. This experience taught me that to design more human AI experiences, we need to go beyond the output by embedding real data to build credibility, allowing interaction to foster engagement, and enabling personalisation to reflect unique user contexts. Designing with these principles brings AI closer to people, not just in utility, but in empathy.

title: Smart Drinking Habit Tracker
lead: DrinkWise is a mobile app designed to help young Australians curb alcohol consumption through personalised support, habit tracking, and healthier social alternatives. As my capstone project for my master's degree, our team tackled the issue of alcohol abuse by creating a solution that promotes long-term behavioural change.

blocks.caption: Directed, filmed, and edited by Jason Yeung

blocks.text: In this project, I led a team of five computer science students, serving as the sole designer and front-end developer. Beyond crafting an intuitive UI and building a cohesive design system, I acted as the bridge between design and development, ensuring seamless implementation. I collaborated closely with developers, collecting feedback to refine interactions and translate designs into practical, scalable solutions. Additionally, I aligned individual contributions with project goals and timelines, reinforcing a strong balance between innovation and feasibility.
Building a strong foundation for collaboration

From the outset, I prioritised understanding my team members’ strengths and backgrounds to foster effective collaboration. Since we had never worked together before, I initiated conversations to align expectations and define clear project goals. To bridge the gap between design and development, I asked three key questions:
- How have you worked with designers in the past?
- How do you think a design can be practically implemented?
- Are there any frameworks you are familiar with and would like to use?

These discussions provided valuable insights into the team’s experience with design and development, shaping how I approached the design process. By understanding their technical preferences and constraints, I tailored the level of design detail to ensure seamless implementation. This early alignment laid the groundwork for an efficient workflow, enabling us to build an intuitive and technically feasible solution together.

When we first embarked on this project, we quickly realised the severity of alcohol overconsumption, especially among young adults. The issue became even more personal when some of our friends were involved in drunk driving incidents, nearly causing accidents and injuries. This firsthand experience reinforced our determination to tackle the problem. Through extensive research, we discovered that social pressure and stress were major contributors to frequent drinking habits, shaping our approach to design a solution that not only tracks alcohol intake but also offers healthier, socially engaging alternatives.

Our design prioritises user freedom after discovering that many young adults feel dissatisfied when products overwhelm them with excessive control or information, especially when addressing personal habits. Instead of taking an intrusive approach, we designed features that gently guide users toward self-awareness and change, ensuring they feel empowered rather than restricted.
Dynamic dashboard – visualising progress for motivation

items.label: User pain point
items.text: Many young adults want to reduce their drinking, but existing apps fail to provide meaningful progress tracking or a sense of achievement when they make positive changes. Without clear feedback, users struggle to stay motivated.

items.label: Goal
items.text: Create a dashboard that offers real-time insights into drinking patterns, reinforcing progress with positive reinforcement and actionable feedback.

items.label: Design solution
items.text:
- Tracks users’ goals and shows weekly achievements to reinforce motivation.
- Displays drinking activity reduction trends for self-awareness.
- Provides cumulative progress tracking since app adoption.
- Sends push notifications to report milestones and keep users engaged.

blocks.text: Drinking activity log – encouraging self-reflection

items.label: User pain point
items.text: Young adults often neglect or forget their drinking habits, making it difficult for them to reflect on patterns and understand the triggers behind their behaviour. Our research revealed that many interviewees experienced moments of self-reflection but lacked a clear record to analyse their habits.

items.label: Goal
items.text: Introduce a detailed logging system that encourages self-awareness, helping users identify drinking patterns and make more informed choices.

items.label: Design solution
items.text:
- Allows users to log drinking activities with timestamps and contextual details.
- Enables them to review past records, fostering reflection and awareness.
- Contributes to progress tracking, reinforcing accountability.

blocks.text: Personalised social event recommendations – alternatives to drinking

items.label: User pain point
items.text: Many young adults associate alcohol with social confidence and peer acceptance. Some feel pressured to drink in social settings, making it difficult to engage in alcohol-free experiences.

items.label: Goal
items.text: Social engagement without alcohol by recommending fulfilling, alternative activities tailored to users' interests.

items.label: Design solution
items.text:
- Suggests personalised social events based on user preferences.
- Uses push notifications to recommend alternative activities at key moments.
- Reinforces the idea that meaningful social experiences don't have to involve alcohol.

blocks.text: To ensure seamless implementation, I maintained constant communication with the development team throughout the design process. By involving developers early—through discussions on component feasibility, prototype reviews, and UI framework alignment—I gathered valuable feedback that improved technical feasibility.

Since the team was familiar with Tailwind CSS, I customised its design system to match the app’s branding and documented it thoroughly. I believe that as a designer, understanding technical aspects leads to more practical and effective designs. Instead of relying solely on theory, I prefer hands-on experience. To bridge the gap between design and development, I learned the basics of React Native and set up the development environment using Expo Router, ensuring a smoother transition from design to implementation.
To measure the success of DrinkWise, I evaluated the app using key performance indicators, including usability testing, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and direct user feedback.

items.label: Usability testing
items.text: Six interviewees participated in usability testing, where all tasks were completed in under 10 seconds. Users expressed overall confidence in navigating the app, though some suggested the addition of a reward system for goal achievements and the ability to select commonly consumed drinks. The app successfully met usability goals, enabling quick and seamless task completion, which is vital for user engagement.

items.label: System usability scale (SUS)
items.text: The app achieved an average SUS score of 82.08, indicating excellent usability. Participants praised the app's ease of use and intuitive design. However, feedback pointed to inconsistencies in the UI and some cumbersome areas, which will be addressed for further UX refinement.

items.label: Effectiveness
items.text: The app was well-received for helping users track their drinking habits, set limits, and find alternative activities. While most found the notifications helpful, some requested more control over reminder timing. This led to an update allowing users to choose their preferred reminder days. Overall, the app was praised for its effectiveness in reducing alcohol consumption.

items.label: Additional achievements
items.text: The project received a Grade 7 (High Distinction) and was nominated as one of the best solutions among 30+ competing teams. It will be showcased as an exemplary case for future students taking the course.

blocks.text: Wrapping up my Master's degree at UQ with the DrinkWise project has been an incredibly rewarding experience. Leading a cross-disciplinary team of five computer science students, we developed DrinkWise, a mobile app aimed at helping young Australians reduce alcohol consumption through habit tracking and personalised activity suggestions. As the only designer, I learned the importance of being open to new areas, like front-end development, and collaborated closely with the team to create a seamless design system that aligned with technical needs. This project not only honed my design and leadership skills but also fostered team bonding and personal growth. I’m proud of what we achieved and excited to bring these experiences into my future career as a product designer.

title: Four Seasons Hotel: Reservation & Loyalty App
lead: The Four Seasons Hotel app was redesigned to address long-standing user pain points and enhance the overall experience. This redesign focuses on streamlining the reservation process and improving customer retention by integrating a loyalty rewards program to boost engagement and conversions.

blocks.text: Since its launch nine years ago, the Four Seasons Hotel app has lacked updates based on user feedback, resulting in several usability challenges. The reservation process is overly complicated, making it frustrating for users to book seamlessly. Additionally, the lack of a reservation management feature creates inconvenience, preventing guests from modifying or tracking their bookings easily. With limited essential features, the app struggles to drive conversions, while the absence of direct communication channels leaves users feeling disconnected from resort staff. These pain points highlight the need for a comprehensive redesign to enhance usability, improve engagement, and streamline the booking experience.

To ensure a user-centric design, I combined user interviews and persona development to uncover key pain points and expectations. These insights informed design opportunities and guided the creation of a more seamless and intuitive booking experience.
User interviews - insights from four Participants on hotel booking experiences

items.label: Research questions
items.text:
- Can you describe the process when you make a reservation for a hotel room?
- What challenges did you face when browsing/reserving a room?
- What will you do during your stay in a hotel?
- Tell me about last time you used a booking app?

items.label: Insights
items.text:
- Interviewees prefer browsing the accommodations with detailed information, e.g. room photos, facilities, bed types, etc.
- Interviewees prioritise the price of the accommodations.
- Interviewees tend to reserve accommodation with a package including, e.g. breakfast included.

blocks.text: User Personas - defining target users

I created two personas to specify my target user group based on distinct travel needs and behaviours. Jack Leung represents family-oriented travellers who prioritise comfort, service quality, and booking flexibility, while Cecilia Cheung reflects young professionals seeking luxury experiences with seamless digital interactions. These personas help me refine the design to address their specific needs.

To inform my design decisions, I developed low-fidelity prototypes from initial sketches and conducted usability tests with five participants aged 20 to 55. Based on the feedback, I analysed the data and identified key areas for improvement, which led to updates such as a streamlined payment module, an enhanced booking confirmation page, and added filtering and sorting features for a more intuitive user experience.

items.label: Insights
items.text:
- Users want easier and more accessible payment
- Users want a booking confirmation page for verification
- Users want more control over search
- Users prefer using a calendar for dates

items.label: Changes made
items.text:
- Redesigned payment experience to a module, making payment details accessible on a single page.
- Enhanced the booking confirmation page, allowing users to confirm details more easily.
- Added sorting and filtering features for better control and more effective searching.
- Introduced a calendar interface for selecting check-in and check-out dates for better usability.

sections.label: Redesigning to address existing user problems

blocks.text: The final app features have been designed with a high-fidelity prototype, aligning closely with the Four Seasons branding. The new design effectively addresses existing user problems, providing an enhanced and intuitive experience.
Optimising search & relevant information display

items.label: User pain point
items.text: The original design lacked an efficient way for users to search for accommodations based on key criteria like date, location, and group size. Instead, users had to manually browse through different locations in a gallery, making it difficult to find suitable options quickly. This resulted in a time-consuming and frustrating experience.

items.label: Goal
items.text: Users need a more effective and straightforward way to search for accommodations based on their specific requirements. Additionally, they should be able to view relevant and useful information while keeping the search functionality easily accessible.

items.label: Design solutions
items.text:
- Redesigned the landing page to display relevant and useful information.
- Integrated an easily accessible search feature for quick and efficient accommodation discovery.
- Streamlined the search process to enhance usability and reduce friction.

blocks.text: Streamlining booking management for a hassle-free experience

items.label: User pain point
items.text: The original design allows users to check in via the app but lacks essential details like booking information, pricing, and the hotel’s exact location. Users also cannot modify or cancel their bookings, often leading to frustrating and unsuccessful attempts to contact customer service.

items.label: Goal
items.text: Users need a seamless way to track, manage, and modify their bookings. They also want the ability to share reservation details easily.

items.label: Design solutions
items.text:
- Introduced a centralised Reservation History page for quick access to all bookings.
- Enabled users to track upcoming stays, view booking history, and access important trip details in one place.
- Added options to modify or cancel bookings, reducing reliance on customer service.

blocks.text: Boosting engagement through exclusive rewards

items.label: User pain point
items.text: Low user retention and engagement due to a lack of incentives for repeat bookings and the absence of attractive offers.

items.label: Goal
items.text: Encourage loyalty by offering exclusive perks and rewards to returning users, enhancing their overall experience and engagement.

items.label: Design solutions
items.text:
- Introduced a loyalty program where users earn points based on their bookings and transactions at Four Seasons hotels.

sections.label: Ensuring design consistency with a comprehensive style guide

blocks.text: To ensure design consistency and brand alignment, I developed a comprehensive style guide and created smart components to maintain uniformity throughout the high-fidelity prototype.

This project helped me apply the knowledge from the Google UX course to a real-world scenario, reinforcing key lessons on user-centric design. Initially, I believed my design would meet users' needs, but usability testing revealed minor issues that I hadn't anticipated. This taught me that user experience is personal and subjective, and we must avoid biases in our designs. Understanding users' true needs was challenging, but it highlighted the importance of being open-minded and putting the user at the centre of the design process. Conducting usability studies was the most rewarding part, showing me that effective design priorities functionality and usability over aesthetics.

title: Fillfull: E-Commerce for Snacks
lead: Fill Full is an e-commerce platform specialising in snack retail, designed to cater to busy professionals, families, and health-conscious individuals in Hong Kong. The website aims to provide a convenient and enjoyable shopping experience by offering a wide selection of snacks, all while focusing on user-centric design.

blocks.text: My work encompassed everything from creating design guidelines to developing a responsive website and implementing user-centred optimisations. It went beyond UX/UI design, also incorporating data analysis and web development. The following content highlights the key features and milestones I delivered throughout the project.

I developed design guidelines for the team to follow, covering image dimensions, brand style, and material file sizes. Before I joined, content was created freely, so material on the website was inconsistent. Image file sizes were large, marketing materials did not align with the brand colours, and some campaign pages were off from the brand vision.
More than 60% of our users access the site on mobile (according to Google Analytics), so I designed and developed the website to be responsive, supporting desktop, tablet, and mobile viewports.
To improve the user experience by tailoring each user’s shopping preferences and turning their interests into conversions, I own the product recommendation module from design through to development.
I also act as a researcher, regularly analysing data from Google Analytics and Hotjar to identify patterns, trends, and opportunities that guide the business direction.

Over 8 months working on this website, I contributed to several impactful changes that positively influenced the project's success. These impacts are reflected in user survey feedback, as well as data from Google Analytics and Shopify.

blocks.text: Throughout this project, collaboration played a key role in shaping the final outcome. I worked closely with the marketing team and graphic designers to ensure their expectations and requirements were fully understood and integrated into the design. Storytelling was an essential skill for presenting my ideas, making them more relatable and engaging for the team. Additionally, taking a data-driven approach was crucial in making the UX improvements measurable. By using data, I was able to validate my hypotheses and demonstrate the real impact of the changes, which made the process even more rewarding.
